common_name: Braeburn Apple (Crisp Aromatic New Zealand Sweet-Tart Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Braeburn needs roughly 700–800 chill hours and a compatible pollinator such as Gala or Golden Delicious flowering at the same time.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun and provide a cross-pollinator, since Braeburn is not reliably self-fruitful. Discovered as a chance seedling near Motueka, New Zealand in 1952, it quickly became one of the most widely exported dessert apples of the late 20th century for its dense, crisp flesh and layered sweet-tart flavor with a faint spice note. Fruit ripens late in the season and colors in streaky red over a green-gold background; it keeps exceptionally well in cold storage, often holding good eating quality for months. Thin heavy fruit sets in early summer to improve size and prevent biennial bearing.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension

common_name: Cripps Pink Apple (Pink Lady, Late-Season Low-Chill Sweet-Tart Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Cripps Pink has a comparatively low chill requirement (around 400–500 hours) and needs a very long, warm growing season to ripen fully, so it is best suited to areas with mild winters and hot, extended autumns.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator, since this cultivar is not self-fertile. Bred by John Cripps in Western Australia from a cross of Golden Delicious and Lady Williams, it is marketed commercially as Pink Lady and is among the latest-ripening apples grown, often left on the tree into late autumn to fully develop its rosy-pink blush and dense, crisp, sweet-tart flesh. Its lower chill requirement compared to classic northern apples makes it one of the more workable dessert apples for warmer growing regions. Fruit stores exceptionally well and resists browning better than many varieties once cut.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension

common_name: Arkansas Black Apple (Ozark Heirloom Dark-Skinned Keeper Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Arkansas Black has a fairly high chill requirement (800+ hours) and needs a pollinator such as Winesap or Stayman.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator variety. This late-1800s Ozark heirloom is famous for skin that darkens from deep red to nearly black in full sun, and for fruit that is rock-hard and tart at harvest but mellows into a dense, sweet, aromatic apple after two to three months in storage. Because of this, growers pick it in October and cellar it rather than eating it fresh off the tree. The thick skin and firm flesh make it an outstanding long-keeping cider and baking apple that was once a major shipping variety before modern refrigeration existed.

common_name: Mutsu Apple (Crispin, Large Honeyed Japanese-Bred Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Mutsu is a triploid and produces very little viable pollen, so it needs two different diploid pollinator varieties planted nearby rather than a single partner.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible diploid pollinator varieties nearby, since triploid cultivars cannot pollinate themselves or each other. Bred in Aomori Prefecture, Japan from a cross involving Golden Delicious and released in the late 1940s, Mutsu produces very large, greenish-yellow fruit with dense, juicy flesh and a rich, honeyed sweetness that intensifies in storage. It is sold in Britain and parts of Europe under the name Crispin. The tree is vigorous and productive, and the fruit holds its shape well when baked, making it a favorite for pies alongside fresh eating.
sources: Washington State University Tree Fruit Extension
Penn State Extension — Tree Fruit Production Guide

common_name: Ein Shemer Apple (Very Low-Chill Gulf South Apple for Zone 8-9)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Ein Shemer needs only about 300 chill hours, making it one of the few apples that reliably fruits in the Gulf South, and it doubles as an effective pollinator for Anna and Dorsett Golden, which bloom at a similar time.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; unlike most apples, Ein Shemer was selected in Israel specifically for regions with mild, short winters and thrives where classic high-chill apples like Red Delicious or Fuji fail to break dormancy properly. The medium, yellow-green fruit is mild and sweet with a soft, quick-to-ripen texture, best eaten soon after picking rather than stored long term. It ripens early in the season, generally ahead of most other low-chill apples, and its abundant, well-timed bloom makes it a valuable cross-pollinator in a mixed low-chill apple planting. This is one of the more dependable apple choices for zone 9a gardens along the Gulf Coast.
